etymology: English surname likely from a Norman-French root for “a swelling” or “a cushion”; the given name John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Bunyan (1628–1688), the Bedford tinker turned Particular Baptist preacher, stands among the brightest witnesses God raised from the lowly. Unlettered by the world’s reckoning, he was schooled in the school of Christ through deep conviction of sin, recounted in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, where the LORD brought him from terror to settled assurance in free grace. Refusing to silence his preaching at the crown’s command, he was imprisoned in Bedford gaol for twelve years rather than promise to cease declaring the gospel. There, in confinement, he penned The Pilgrim’s Progress, the allegory of Christian’s journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City—a book that, under God, has carried the way of salvation to more souls than any volume save Scripture itself. His doctrine was thoroughly that of the doctrines of grace: man dead in trespasses, sovereign election, the all-sufficiency of Christ’s blood, and perseverance to the end. Bunyan did not soften the narrow gate nor the burden that only the cross can loose. His life answers the lie that learning or station qualifies a man to herald Christ; the Spirit equips whom He calls. He preached as a dying man to dying men, and his pilgrim still walks, bidding every reader flee the wrath to come and look to the One who bore it.
webster_summary: An English Particular Baptist preacher and tinker, imprisoned for twelve years, author of The Pilgrim’s Progress, the most widely read Christian allegory.
webster_full: JOHN BUNYAN, English Nonconformist preacher (1628–1688), a tinker of Elstow near Bedford converted out of profanity and despair to assured faith in Christ.
Imprisoned twelve years in Bedford gaol for refusing to cease unlicensed preaching of the gospel.
Author of The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678), the allegory of Christian’s pilgrimage to the Celestial City.
Author of Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, the record of his own conviction and conversion.
A convinced Particular Baptist holding the doctrines of sovereign grace; he counted persecution gain for the sake of preaching Christ (Php 1:29).
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Php 1:29
For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake.
corruption_summary: Bunyan’s pilgrim is now claimed by a vague cultural “journey” sentiment stripped of the gospel of grace that is its whole substance.
corruption_paragraphs: Bunyan’s great allegory is often invoked as a generic metaphor for any “spiritual journey” or self-discovery, the word pilgrim emptied of Christian’s burden, his flight from wrath, and his deliverance at the cross. But Bunyan wrote no parable of self-improvement. His Christian is a guilty sinner fleeing the City of Destruction, saved not by the journey but by the Crucified One at whose feet his burden falls away. To borrow the imagery while denying the doctrine is to keep the road and forsake the Saviour who is its end.

The lesson to recover is that the Christian life is pilgrimage through a hostile world toward a sure city, sustained by sovereign grace and not by the pilgrim’s strength. Bunyan’s pen, sharpened in prison, calls every reader to count the cost, take up the cross, and press on through Vanity Fair and the Slough of Despond to the gate that the Lamb has opened. The pilgrimage is real; so is the wrath fled and the glory sought.
roots_summary: The surname Bunyan is of obscure Norman-French derivation; his given name John carries the meaning “the LORD is gracious.”
roots_lines: John Bunyan — John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious,” fitting for the author of Grace Abounding.
Bunyan, an English surname of uncertain Norman-French origin, possibly from a root meaning “a swelling” or “a hump.”
His trade-name “tinker” marks a mender of pots and kettles, a despised itinerant craft of his day.
Pilgrim, from the Latin peregrinus, “a stranger, a foreigner,” one passing through a land not his own.
Allegory, from the Greek allos (“other”) and agoreuein (“to speak”), a speaking of one thing under the figure of another.
usage: John Bunyan preached the same free grace from the pulpit and from the prison cell.
Generations of believers learned the shape of the Christian life from John Bunyan’s pilgrim.
When pressed to promise silence, John Bunyan answered that he would lie in gaol till the moss grew on his eyelids before he would cease to preach.

etymology: English given name Ralph, from the Old Norse Ráðulfr, “counsel-wolf”; the surname Venning a West-Country place-name.
biblical_def: Ralph Venning (c.1621–1674) was a Puritan minister of Devon stock, educated at Cambridge, who labored in London and was among the nearly two thousand faithful ministers ejected in 1662 for refusing to bow to the Act of Uniformity. He is chiefly remembered for his searching treatise on sin, first titled Sin, the Plague of Plagues and later The Sinfulness of Sin, a work that anatomizes transgression as the believer’s deadliest enemy. Venning’s aim was not to crush the conscience without remedy but to magnify the grace of Christ by setting forth the exceeding sinfulness of sin—that the soul, seeing sin’s true vileness against an infinitely holy God, might flee the more swiftly to the Redeemer. He held the Reformed conviction that sin is no mere weakness or misfortune but rebellion against the Most High, deserving wrath, and curable only by the blood of the Lamb. His pastoral tenderness joined to doctrinal severity marks the true physician of souls, who shows the wound before he applies the balm. Ejected and silenced by the world, Venning nonetheless ministered grace through his pen, teaching the church to hate what God hates and to prize the cross that alone removes guilt. His witness stands as a rebuke to every age that would make light of sin and so make light of the Saviour.
webster_summary: An ejected Puritan minister of London, author of The Sinfulness of Sin (formerly Sin, the Plague of Plagues), a classic anatomy of transgression.
webster_full: RALPH VENNING, English Puritan minister (c.1621–1674), educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and a preacher in London.
Among the ministers ejected in 1662 for refusing conformity to the Act of Uniformity.
Author of Sin, the Plague of Plagues, afterward republished as The Sinfulness of Sin.
His treatise sets forth sin as the soul’s deadliest enemy and rebellion against a holy God (Rom 7:13).
He magnified the grace of Christ by exposing the true vileness of transgression.
scriptures: Rom 7:13
Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Rom 6:23
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.
corruption_summary: Venning’s doctrine of sin is recovered against an age that renames transgression as weakness, sickness, or social conditioning.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Venning’s great theme stands directly athwart the spirit of the present age, which will not call sin sin. Where Scripture and Venning name rebellion against a holy God, the modern temper substitutes “poor choices,” “mistakes,” or the fault of circumstance, and so dissolves guilt into mere misfortune. But a sin that is only sickness needs no Saviour, only therapy; Venning’s anatomy of the sinfulness of sin is the necessary cure for that flattery.

The lesson to recover is that sin must be seen in its true vileness before grace appears in its true sweetness. Venning showed the wound that the balm of Christ might be prized. A church that minimizes sin will inevitably minimize the cross; one that, with Venning, trembles at sin’s exceeding sinfulness will run the harder to the blood that washes it away.
roots_summary: The name Ralph means “counsel-wolf” from the Norse; Venning is a West-Country English surname.
roots_lines: Ralph — from Old Norse Ráðulfr, “counsel” joined to “wolf.”
Venning, an English surname rooted in Devon and the West Country.
Plague, from the Latin plaga, “a blow, a stroke,” hence a deadly affliction.
Sin, from the Old English synn, used to render the Hebrew chatta’ah and Greek hamartia, “a missing of the mark.”
Sinfulness intensifies the noun, marking sin’s essential and exceeding wickedness (Rom 7:13).
usage: Ralph Venning taught the church to see sin as the plague of plagues.
After his ejection in 1662, Ralph Venning ministered chiefly through his pen.
No writer exposes the true vileness of transgression more searchingly than Ralph Venning.

etymology: English given name William, from the Germanic Wilhelm, “resolute protector”; the surname Bridge from the Old English brycg, a crossing over water.
biblical_def: William Bridge (c.1600–1671) was a Puritan minister and one of the divines summoned to the Westminster Assembly, where he stood among the “dissenting brethren” who pressed the Congregational way of church order against the Presbyterian majority. Educated at Cambridge, he fled to Holland under Laudian persecution and pastored an English congregation at Rotterdam before returning to labor at Yarmouth. Though he differed with his brethren on polity, he was one with them in the doctrines of grace and in warm experimental godliness. His most enduring work, A Lifting Up for the Downcast, is a treasury of comfort for the cast-down believer, addressing the soul discouraged by sin, by affliction, by desertion, by want of assurance, and by the wickedness of the heart. Bridge brings the promises of God to bear upon each particular grief, insisting that no condition of the saint lies beyond the reach of Christ’s sufficiency. He held that discouragement dishonors God by doubting His faithfulness, and so he labored to lift the eyes of the weary from their wounds to their Physician. A faithful preacher and a tender pastor, Bridge embodies the Puritan gift of joining doctrinal precision to the cure of troubled consciences, pointing fainting pilgrims to the unfailing grace that sustains them to the end.
webster_summary: A Puritan minister and Westminster divine of the Congregational party, author of A Lifting Up for the Downcast.
webster_full: WILLIAM BRIDGE, English Puritan minister (c.1600–1671), educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.
Fled to Rotterdam under Laudian persecution, returning to pastor at Great Yarmouth.
One of the divines of the Westminster Assembly and a leader of the Congregational “dissenting brethren.”
Author of A Lifting Up for the Downcast, a classic of pastoral comfort for the discouraged soul.
He taught that no affliction of the saint lies beyond the sufficiency of Christ (2Co 4:8).
scriptures: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Bridge’s ministry of comfort is recovered against a therapeutic age that treats discouragement as a chemical problem rather than a matter for the promises of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Bridge’s pastoral work confronts the modern habit of reducing every cast-down soul to a mere imbalance to be medicated, severed from God, conscience, and the promises of Scripture. Bridge did not deny real affliction; he addressed it with the whole counsel of God, naming the soul’s discouragements one by one and answering each with the sufficiency of Christ. To lift the downcast by the gospel is a richer cure than the world’s, for it touches the spirit and not merely the frame.

The lesson to recover is that discouragement, however heavy, is no place beyond the reach of grace, and that to doubt God’s faithfulness dishonors Him. Bridge teaches the weary believer to argue with his own soul as the psalmist did, to hope in God, and to wait upon the LORD who renews the strength of the faint. The remedy for the downcast is not within the self but above it, in the unfailing mercy of Christ.
roots_summary: William means “resolute protector”; Bridge denotes a crossing, a fitting name for one who pointed souls over from despair to hope.
roots_lines: William — from Germanic Wilhelm, “will” joined to “helmet,” hence “resolute protector.”
Bridge, from Old English brycg, a structure spanning water.
Downcast, from down and cast, the soul thrown low, as in “cast down” (Psa 42:11).
Comfort, from the Latin confortare, “to strengthen greatly,” not merely to soothe.
Dissenting, from the Latin dissentire, “to differ in judgment,” as Bridge dissented on church order.
usage: William Bridge wrote to lift up the souls that affliction had cast down.
Among the Westminster divines, William Bridge contended for the Congregational way.
When despair pressed hard, the saints found in William Bridge a faithful physician of the soul.

etymology: Hebrew given name David, “beloved”; the surname Clarkson, “son of the clerk” or scholar.
biblical_def: David Clarkson (1622–1686) was a Puritan minister and scholar, educated at Cambridge, who labored faithfully through the upheavals of his age and was ejected in 1662 with the host of Nonconformist ministers who would not bow to the Act of Uniformity. In his later years he served as colleague and then successor to the great John Owen at the congregation in London, no small honor, for Owen esteemed him highly. Clarkson was a preacher of uncommon weight and a theologian of careful judgment, and several of his sermons endure as choice Puritan divinity. Best known among them is Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven, a piercing exposure of the idolatry that lurks not in carved images alone but in the heart’s inward esteeming, trusting, loving, and fearing of any thing above God. Clarkson showed that whatever the soul prizes more than the LORD, whatever it makes its chief good or its refuge, becomes an idol that bars the gate of heaven. His doctrine pressed the first commandment inward upon the conscience, leaving no covert for secret idols. A man of learning and piety, Clarkson stands among those faithful pastors whom the church remembers chiefly through their printed sermons, ministering still to readers the searching, God-exalting truth they once preached to congregations now long gathered home.
webster_summary: An ejected Puritan minister and successor to John Owen, remembered for the sermon Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven.
webster_full: DAVID CLARKSON, English Puritan minister and scholar (1622–1686), educated at Clare College, Cambridge.
Ejected in 1662 for refusing conformity to the Act of Uniformity.
Colleague and successor of John Owen at his London congregation.
Author of the sermon Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven.
He exposed inward idolatry of heart as the secret transgression of the first commandment (Eze 14:3).
scriptures: Eze 14:3
Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be inquired of at all by them?
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
Exo 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
corruption_summary: Clarkson’s doctrine of soul-idolatry is recovered against an age that confines idolatry to ancient statues and never suspects the idols of the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Clarkson’s great theme rebukes the modern conceit that idolatry is a primitive sin of carved images, long since outgrown. Clarkson showed that the heart is a perpetual factory of idols, and that to love, trust, fear, or esteem any thing—wealth, reputation, pleasure, self—above God is soul-idolatry, the inward breaking of the first commandment. The polished modern who scoffs at heathen shrines may yet bow before idols of his own affection.

The lesson to recover is that worship is the deepest act of the soul, and that whatever it makes its chief good it makes its god. Clarkson presses the conscience to ask not merely what it bows before in temples but what it cherishes, relies upon, and dreads to lose. The remedy is to dethrone every rival and to give to God alone the supreme love, trust, and fear that are His due.
roots_summary: David means “beloved”; Clarkson means “son of the clerk,” the scholar.
roots_lines: David — from Hebrew Dawid, “beloved.”
Clarkson, “son of the clerk,” from clerk, anciently a learned man or cleric.
Idol, from the Greek eidōlon, “an image, a phantom,” a false object of worship.
Idolatry, the service or worship rendered to an idol, whether outward or inward (Col 3:5).
Mortify, from the Latin mortificare, “to put to death,” as the saint must slay his idols.
usage: David Clarkson preached that the heart’s secret idols shut men out of heaven.
John Owen esteemed David Clarkson enough to make him his colleague and successor.
After his ejection, David Clarkson’s searching sermons endured in print.

etymology: Given name from the Greco-Roman hero Hercules; the surname Collins, a patronymic from Colin, a diminutive of Nicholas, “victory of the people.”
biblical_def: Hercules Collins (d.1702) was a Particular Baptist pastor in London, shepherd of the Wapping (later Old Gravel Lane) congregation, and a stout contender for the faith in a season of fierce persecution against the Nonconformists. He is best remembered for An Orthodox Catechism (1680), a careful Baptist adaptation of the venerable Heidelberg Catechism, in which Collins took the rich, comforting teaching of that Reformed standard and revised its articles on the sacraments to accord with the conviction that baptism belongs to believers alone, administered by immersion. By this labor he showed that the Particular Baptists were no novel sect but heirs of the Reformation, confessing the same gospel of free grace as the Reformed churches while ordering the ordinances by Scripture. Collins belonged to the circle of pastors who held and propagated the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689, the great Particular Baptist standard, and he suffered imprisonment for his faithful preaching. A man of pastoral zeal and confessional conviction, he labored to ground his people in sound doctrine and to defend believer’s baptism as the apostolic pattern. His Orthodox Catechism remains a witness that the Baptists of his day were confessional, catechetical, and thoroughly Reformed in the doctrines of grace.
webster_summary: A London Particular Baptist pastor, author of An Orthodox Catechism, a Baptist adaptation of the Heidelberg Catechism.
webster_full: HERCULES COLLINS, English Particular Baptist pastor (d.1702) of the Wapping congregation in London.
Author of An Orthodox Catechism (1680), adapting the Heidelberg Catechism to Baptist conviction.
Within the circle of pastors who confessed the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689.
Imprisoned for his faithful preaching during the persecution of the Nonconformists.
He defended believer’s baptism by immersion as the apostolic pattern (Act 8:38).
scriptures: Act 8:38
And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
corruption_summary: Collins’ catechetical labor is recovered against an age that despises catechism and severs the Baptists from their confessional, Reformed heritage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Collins’ work answers two errors common today: the notion that catechizing is dead formalism, and the notion that Baptists are a doctrineless people with no confessional roots. Collins took the Heidelberg Catechism, the warm and comforting standard of the Reformed, and made it serve a Baptist congregation, proving that the Particular Baptists were Reformed in the doctrines of grace and differed only where Scripture led them on the subjects and mode of baptism.

The lesson to recover is the recovery of catechism itself—the patient grounding of God’s people, young and old, in sound doctrine through question and answer. Collins also recovers for modern Baptists the memory that they are heirs of the Reformation and confessors of the 1689, not a sect cut loose from history. To catechize is to obey the charge to teach all nations; to confess is to hold fast the form of sound words.
roots_summary: Hercules is the name of the classical hero; Collins descends from a diminutive of Nicholas, “victory of the people.”
roots_lines: Hercules — from the Greek Heraklēs, the famed hero of strength.
Collins, a patronymic from Colin, diminutive of Nicholas, “victory of the people.”
Catechism, from the Greek katēchein, “to sound down, to instruct by word of mouth.”
Orthodox, from the Greek orthos (“right”) and doxa (“opinion, glory”), hence “right belief.”
Baptize, from the Greek baptizō, “to immerse, to dip” (Act 8:38).
usage: Hercules Collins adapted the Heidelberg Catechism for a Baptist congregation.
By An Orthodox Catechism, Hercules Collins showed Baptists to be confessional and Reformed.
Hercules Collins suffered imprisonment rather than abandon his pulpit.

etymology: Hebrew given name Abraham, “father of a multitude”; the surname Booth, from the Old Norse búð, “a dwelling or shelter.”
biblical_def: Abraham Booth (1734–1806) was an eighteenth-century Particular Baptist pastor who served the congregation at Prescot Street, London, for nearly forty years. Reared in humble circumstances and largely self-taught, Booth was for a season inclined to the doctrine of general redemption, but upon deeper searching of the Scriptures he was brought to embrace the doctrines of sovereign grace, and out of that conviction he wrote his enduring work, The Reign of Grace. In it he traces the dominion of grace from its eternal source in election, through the cross of Christ, into the regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, and final perseverance of the saints, showing at every step that grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life and that salvation from first to last is the free gift of God. Booth set grace in deliberate contrast to all schemes of human merit, insisting that the believer owes everything to the unmerited favor of the LORD. He was esteemed among his brethren as a man of integrity, doctrinal soundness, and pastoral diligence, and he contended earnestly against errors that would dishonor free grace. His writings, marked by clarity and scriptural fullness, ministered to his own generation and to many since, exalting the God who saves to the praise of the glory of His grace and abasing the pride of man, who has nothing he did not first receive.
webster_summary: An eighteenth-century Particular Baptist pastor of London, author of The Reign of Grace.
webster_full: ABRAHAM BOOTH, English Particular Baptist pastor (1734–1806), minister at Prescot Street, London, for nearly forty years.
Largely self-taught, he turned from general redemption to the doctrines of sovereign grace.
Author of The Reign of Grace, tracing grace from election to final perseverance.
He set free grace against every scheme of human merit (Rom 5:21).
Esteemed among his brethren for integrity, sound doctrine, and pastoral diligence.
scriptures: Rom 5:21
That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Tit 2:11
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Booth’s doctrine of reigning grace is recovered against an age that hollows the word “grace” into mere niceness or general tolerance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the word at the heart of Booth’s labor is constantly counterfeited. The world borrows “grace” to mean a vague kindliness, an easy tolerance, or a pardon that costs nothing and changes nothing. Booth’s Reign of Grace recovers the biblical meaning: unmerited favor that reigns through righteousness, purchased by the blood of Christ and applied sovereignly to the elect, transforming as well as forgiving.

The lesson to recover is that grace is a reigning power, not a passive sentiment—it dethrones sin, justifies the guilty, and carries the saint to glory. Booth set grace against all merit precisely so that God should have all the praise. Where the present age cheapens grace into mere leniency, Booth restores it as the costly, conquering favor of God that saves from first to last.
roots_summary: Abraham means “father of a multitude”; Booth denotes a shelter or dwelling.
roots_lines: Abraham — from Hebrew Abraham, “father of a multitude.”
Booth, from Old Norse búð, “a temporary dwelling or shelter.”
Grace, from the Latin gratia, rendering the Greek charis, “unmerited favor.”
Reign, from the Latin regnare, “to rule as king,” as grace reigns through righteousness (Rom 5:21).
Redemption, from the Latin redimere, “to buy back,” the price Booth saw fixed by sovereign grace.
usage: Abraham Booth traced the reign of grace from election to glory.
Once inclined to general redemption, Abraham Booth came to confess sovereign grace.
For nearly forty years Abraham Booth shepherded the Prescot Street congregation.

etymology: Hebrew given name Matthew, “gift of the LORD”; the surname Mead, from the Old English mæd, “a meadow.”
biblical_def: Matthew Mead (c.1630–1699) was a Puritan minister who labored in and around London and was among those silenced by the Act of Uniformity in 1662, afterward continuing as a Nonconformist pastor at Stepney, where he gathered a large and faithful congregation. He is chiefly remembered for his searching treatise The Almost Christian Discovered, drawn from the words of Agrippa to Paul, “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.” In it Mead anatomizes the deceptive condition of the man who goes far in the form of religion yet falls short of saving grace—who has knowledge without holiness, profession without possession, conviction without conversion. With great discernment he marks out the many ways a man may resemble a true believer and yet remain a stranger to Christ: he may hate sin and yet not forsake it, may obey much of the law and yet not be born again, may have great gifts and yet lack the one thing needful. Mead’s aim was to awaken the self-deceived from a false peace and to drive the soul to examine whether it be truly in the faith. His doctrine flows from the Reformed conviction that regeneration is the sovereign work of the Spirit and that no measure of outward religion can supply its place. The treatise remains a sharp instrument for self-examination, sparing no false hope.
webster_summary: A silenced Puritan minister of Stepney, author of The Almost Christian Discovered.
webster_full: MATTHEW MEAD, English Puritan minister (c.1630–1699), pastor of a large Nonconformist congregation at Stepney.
Silenced by the Act of Uniformity in 1662 yet continuing to preach.
Author of The Almost Christian Discovered, from Agrippa’s words in Act 26:28.
He anatomized the self-deceived professor who has form without saving grace.
His doctrine rested on regeneration as the sovereign work of the Spirit (Joh 3:3).
scriptures: Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
Joh 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
Mat 7:21
Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Mead’s warning against the “almost Christian” is recovered against an age that calls every professor saved and never tests the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Mead’s subject cuts directly against the modern aversion to self-examination, which treats any call to prove one’s faith as harsh or judgmental. Mead, following Paul’s charge to examine ourselves, showed how far a man may go in religion—in knowledge, profession, even reformation—and yet remain unconverted. To flatter the almost Christian into false peace is the cruelest kindness; to discover him is mercy.

The lesson to recover is the necessity of the new birth and the duty of honest self-examination. Mead teaches that the gate to false hope is wide, and that many who say “Lord, Lord” have never been made new by the Spirit. The remedy is not to multiply outward religion but to be born again, and to prove, by Scripture and conscience, whether Christ be truly formed within.
roots_summary: Matthew means “gift of the LORD”; Mead denotes a meadow.
roots_lines: Matthew — from Hebrew Mattithyahu, “gift of the LORD.”
Mead, from Old English mæd, “a meadow, a tract of grassland.”
Almost, from all and most, “very nearly,” the perilous nearness of Agrippa (Act 26:28).
Hypocrite, from the Greek hypokritēs, “an actor,” one who plays a part not truly his own.
Regeneration, from the Latin regeneratio, “a being born again” (Joh 3:3).
usage: Matthew Mead exposed the man who is almost, but not altogether, a Christian.
Silenced in 1662, Matthew Mead still gathered a great congregation at Stepney.
Few books search the conscience like Matthew Mead’s Almost Christian Discovered.

etymology: Greek given name George, “husbandman, tiller of the soil”; the surname Swinnock, an English place- or occupational name.
biblical_def: George Swinnock (c.1627–1673) was a Puritan minister, educated at Cambridge and Oxford, who labored at several parishes before he too was ejected in 1662 under the Act of Uniformity, thereafter ministering privately as a Nonconformist. His most considerable work, The Christian Man’s Calling, is a vast and practical treatise on the duty of godliness in every station and circumstance of life. Swinnock’s great burden was that true religion is not confined to the closet or the Sabbath but must govern the whole man—in his employment and recreation, his prosperity and adversity, his eating and sleeping, his marriage and his calling, his sickness and his dying. He held, with the Puritan school, that the believer is to do all to the glory of God, and he labored to show how the most ordinary actions may be sanctified and turned to holy ends. His writing is rich in homely illustration and pointed application, pressing heart-religion upon the conscience without lapsing into mere external rule-keeping. Swinnock united doctrinal soundness with experimental warmth, insisting that godliness is the Christian’s whole business, the calling above every earthly calling. His works minister still to those who would learn to walk with God not only in the sanctuary but through all the common ways of life, redeeming the time and living unto Him who bought them.
webster_summary: An ejected Puritan minister, author of The Christian Man’s Calling, a practical treatise on godliness in every station of life.
webster_full: GEORGE SWINNOCK, English Puritan minister (c.1627–1673), educated at Cambridge and Oxford.
Ejected in 1662 under the Act of Uniformity, ministering thereafter as a Nonconformist.
Author of The Christian Man’s Calling, on godliness in every circumstance of life.
He taught that true religion governs the whole man, not the Sabbath alone (1Co 10:31).
His writing joins homely illustration to pointed, heart-searching application.
scriptures: Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Col 3:17
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Swinnock’s vision of whole-life godliness is recovered against an age that privatizes faith and severs Sunday from the rest of the week.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Swinnock’s theme confronts the modern habit of penning religion into a private compartment, kept apart from work, leisure, and the common business of life. Swinnock would have none of it: the Christian man’s calling is to glorify God in everything—in his trade, his table, his marriage, his sickness, his death. To make faith a Sunday affair and the rest of the week one’s own is to deny the lordship of Christ over the whole man.

The lesson to recover is that godliness is the believer’s chief calling, above and through every earthly one, and that the most ordinary deeds may be done to the glory of God. Swinnock teaches the saint to redeem the time and to sanctify common life by holy ends. There is no neutral hour; all of life is to be lived coram Deo, before the face of God, in the name of the Lord Jesus.
roots_summary: George means “husbandman” or tiller of the soil; Swinnock is an English place-derived surname.
roots_lines: George — from the Greek geōrgos, “earth-worker, husbandman.”
Swinnock, an English surname likely of place or occupational origin.
Calling, the rendering of the Greek klēsis, the vocation to which God appoints a man.
Godliness, from God and the suffix -liness, rendering the Greek eusebeia, “true piety” (1Ti 4:8).
Redeem, from the Latin redimere, “to buy back,” as the saint redeems the time (Eph 5:16).
usage: George Swinnock taught that the Christian’s calling reaches into every corner of life.
After his ejection, George Swinnock pressed whole-life godliness through his pen.
George Swinnock would have no man keep his religion for the Sabbath only.

etymology: Hebrew given name John, “the LORD is gracious”; the surname Trapp, of English origin, perhaps from a topographic or occupational root.
biblical_def: John Trapp (1601–1669) was a Puritan minister and schoolmaster of Warwickshire, famed above all for his commentary upon the whole Bible, a vast labor of pithy, witty, and pointed annotation. Educated at Oxford, Trapp served as a parish minister and chaplain through the turbulent years of the Civil War, and his learning ranged widely through the Scriptures and the writers of antiquity. His exposition is unlike the weighty discursive commentaries of some of his brethren; it sparkles with terse epigram, homely proverb, and a quickness of phrase that has delighted and instructed readers for generations. Yet beneath the wit lies sound doctrine and a reverent submission to the text, for Trapp aimed always to open the sense of Scripture and press it home upon the conscience. He held the Reformed faith of his age and esteemed the written Word as the very oracles of God, to be searched and obeyed. Later preachers, Spurgeon among them, prized Trapp’s commentary for its rare blend of brevity and savor, calling it a mine of quaint sayings and sound sense. Trapp stands among those faithful expositors who served the church not by ruling congregations alone but by laying open the whole counsel of God in print, that the people might feed upon the Scriptures with both profit and delight.
webster_summary: A Puritan minister and commentator famed for his pithy, witty annotations upon the whole Bible.
webster_full: JOHN TRAPP, English Puritan minister and schoolmaster (1601–1669) of Warwickshire, educated at Oxford.
Author of a celebrated commentary upon the whole Bible, marked by terse and witty annotation.
A parish minister and chaplain through the years of the English Civil War.
His exposition joins quickness of phrase to sound Reformed doctrine.
Later esteemed by Spurgeon as a mine of quaint sayings and solid sense (Psa 119:103).
scriptures: How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
corruption_summary: Trapp’s reverent, witty exposition is recovered against an age that treats the Bible as ancient literature rather than the very oracles of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Trapp’s lifework stands against the modern reduction of Scripture to mere ancient literature, dissected for human authorship and cultural conditioning rather than searched as the inspired Word. Trapp’s wit never trifled with the text; his quick sayings served a deep reverence for the oracles of God, to be obeyed and not merely studied. His commentary feeds faith because it submits to the Scripture it expounds.

The lesson to recover is that the Bible is sweet to the taste of the believing soul, profitable for doctrine and life, and worthy of both diligent study and holy delight. Trapp shows that learning and liveliness need not quench reverence—that a fitly spoken word, like apples of gold, may carry sound doctrine far. The church is well served by expositors who, like Trapp, open the sense of Scripture and press it sweetly home.
roots_summary: John means “the LORD is gracious”; Trapp is an English surname of uncertain root.
roots_lines: John — from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”
Trapp, an English surname, perhaps from a topographic or occupational origin.
Commentary, from the Latin commentarium, “a note-book, a memorandum,” an exposition of a text.
Annotation, from the Latin annotare, “to mark, to note down.”
Pithy, from pith, the inner substance, hence concise and full of meaning (Pro 25:11).
usage: John Trapp packed more wit into a line of commentary than most writers into a page.
Spurgeon kept John Trapp near at hand for his quaint and savory sense.
John Trapp opened the whole Bible with pithy and pointed annotations.

etymology: Aramaic given name Thomas, “a twin”; the surname Shepard, a variant of shepherd, “one who tends sheep.”
biblical_def: Thomas Shepard (1605–1649) was an English-born Puritan who, driven from his homeland by Laudian persecution, crossed to New England and became the founding pastor of the church at Cambridge in Massachusetts, hard by the new college that would be named Harvard. Educated at Cambridge in England, Shepard was a preacher of singular searching power and a leading figure in the spiritual life of the early colony. He is remembered for his treatises The Sincere Convert and The Sound Believer, and above all for The Parable of the Ten Virgins Opened and Applied, a great body of sermons upon Matthew twenty-five that anatomizes the difference between the wise and foolish, the true believer and the false professor. Shepard preached preparation, conviction, and the absolute necessity of regenerating grace, refusing all false comfort and pressing his hearers to examine whether their oil was the genuine work of the Spirit or a mere outward profession that would fail at the bridegroom’s coming. He took a leading part against the antinomian errors that troubled the colony, contending for sound doctrine joined to holy life. His Autobiography and Journal reveal a heart of deep humility and self-jealousy before God. Shepard stands among the choicest of the New England divines, a faithful shepherd who fed the flock and warned the careless, exalting sovereign grace and the necessity of the new birth.
webster_summary: A New England Puritan, founding pastor at Cambridge, author of The Sincere Convert and The Parable of the Ten Virgins.
webster_full: THOMAS SHEPARD, English-born Puritan (1605–1649), founding pastor of the church at Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Driven to New England by Laudian persecution, educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.
Author of The Sincere Convert, The Sound Believer, and The Parable of the Ten Virgins.
A leading opponent of the antinomian errors that troubled the early colony.
He pressed conviction, preparation, and the necessity of regenerating grace (Mat 25:13).
scriptures: Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
Mat 25:4
But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Shepard’s searching call to true conversion is recovered against an age of easy assurance that never tests whether the lamp holds oil.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Shepard’s ministry rebukes the modern aversion to self-examination and the cheap assurance that pronounces every professor saved. Shepard opened the parable of the ten virgins to show that the foolish, too, had lamps and a profession, yet wanted the oil of true grace and were shut out at the last. He refused false comfort and pressed his hearers to prove whether Christ was truly in them, knowing that a hope untried is a hope undone.

The lesson to recover is the necessity of the new birth and of watchfulness against the bridegroom’s coming. Shepard teaches that men may resemble the saved in much and yet be strangers to regenerating grace; therefore the soul must examine itself and seek the genuine oil of the Spirit. To watch, to be ready, to be truly converted—this is no harsh demand but the mercy of a faithful shepherd warning the careless of the door that shuts.
roots_summary: Thomas means “a twin”; Shepard is a variant of shepherd, “one who tends the flock.”
roots_lines: Thomas — from Aramaic T’oma, “a twin.”
Shepard, a variant of shepherd, from Old English scēaphierde, “sheep-herder.”
Convert, from the Latin convertere, “to turn about,” one turned from sin to God.
Virgin, from the Latin virgo, here the ten of the parable awaiting the bridegroom (Mat 25:13).
Watch, rendering the Greek grēgoreite, “be vigilant, stay awake” (Mat 25:13).
usage: Thomas Shepard opened the parable of the ten virgins to test every false profession.
Driven from England, Thomas Shepard founded the church at Cambridge in New England.
Thomas Shepard preached the new birth with a searching power few could equal.
